recap_lines: Clarity is telling what is going on, and satisfaction is feeling good to act.

bookends.command: Quiz me on game art terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms clarity, satisfaction, visual hierarchy, contrast, silhouette, readability, reference, mood board, proxy model and low-poly mesh. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

In this made-up example a thing counts as readable at sixteen pixels or more and three to one contrast, and only four of the eight pass. For example, a spike trap drawn in the same brown as the floor fails clarity, because the player sees the danger only after landing on it.

beats.narration_text: Satisfaction means each action gets a quick, responsive answer, so acting feels good. Both squares answer the same press. In this made-up example the fast one answers in forty milliseconds, and the slow one in seven hundred, six hundred sixty later, and it lags. Clarity asks whether you can tell what is going on. Satisfaction asks whether it feels good to act. For example, a coin that pops and chimes the instant the player touches it is satisfying.

beats.narration_text: Six circles, and a bar for each. Visual hierarchy means arranging a picture so the most important things are seen first, then the next, in order. Here attention is scored as size times contrast, a simple stand-in. The boss gets forty-six percent, the player twenty-two, the rock only three. Contrast is one difference, and hierarchy is the order the eye visits. For example, on a title menu the Start button should be seen first, the options next, and the credits last.

beats.narration_text: Contrast is any difference that pulls the eye to one place, and it can be measured. Three colour pairs sit on a scale from one to twenty-one. White on cream is one point one one to one, almost invisible. Dark ink on cream is eleven point two three to one, and black on white is twenty-one to one. For example, a white score number on a pale sky is hard to see, and a dark outline around it raises its contrast.

beats.narration_text: Light and dark contrast is the gap between light and dark areas, with hue taken away. Each colour on top is shown below as its grey. Red and blue look very different, yet both land at zero point one three, almost the same grey. Light and dark contrast survives a black and white copy, and colour alone often does not. For example, turn a level screenshot grey. If a red enemy and a blue floor become one grey, make the enemy much lighter or darker.

beats.narration_text: Silhouette is the outline of an object alone, and it should still say what the object is when filled black at game size. A knight and a blob are filled black and shrunk from forty-eight down to six. The tell-apart score is one minus their overlap, and it stays between zero point four two and zero point five three at every size. For example, fill a new enemy sprite black beside the player, at its size in the level, and check you can still name it.
